title: The era of unbounded products: Designing for Multimodal IO: Ben Hylak
talk_summary: A product-design talk about making 'unbounded' AI interfaces predictable via structure: highlighting what matters, hierarchy, familiarity, pulled-out artifacts, versioning, presets, and per-user personalization.

takeaways.what_they_do: Replace blank-canvas prompting with curated, named presets and examples so users pick a proven configuration rather than hand-writing fragile prompts.
takeaways.evidence_quote: skipping all the sort of noise of prompt hacking prompt engineering are examples and presets

takeaways.technique: Developer-defined tunable parameters over text prompts
takeaways.what_they_do: Expose structured knobs (tone, strictness, etc.) that can be tuned per user/context, because text prompts are brittle.
takeaways.evidence_quote: text prompts are sort of this fragile House of Cards where if you remove one word the whole output changes

takeaways.technique: Pull structured artifacts out of the conversation stream
takeaways.what_they_do: Keep the evolving artifact (app/code) in a separate pane with versions, so follow-up chatter doesn't corrupt or float away the working object.
takeaways.evidence_quote: they pulled out the structure which is the app you're working on and iterating on from the actual conversation

takeaways.what_they_do: Model multi-step agent pipelines as spreadsheet columns (one step per column) with rows as items, run first N rows as an eval then scale.
takeaways.evidence_quote: each column is essentially a step that an agent is taking ... you run the first 10 rows and then you run the next 50,000

takeaways.technique: Shift from evals to per-user analytics
takeaways.what_they_do: For subjective quality dimensions there is no single correct answer, so measure whether outputs meet each user's/context's needs via analytics rather than fixed evals.
takeaways.evidence_quote: shifting from evals to analytics ... the right sort of tone for a summary for a specific user I don't think so
